question: How many ordered pairs of real numbers \((x,y)\) satisfy the following system of equations? \[\begin{cases} ~x+3y&=3 \\ ~\big||x|-|y|\big|&=1 \end{cases}\]
solution:
The signs of \(x\) and \(y\) turn the nested absolute values into simple linear conditions. If \(xy\geq0\), then
\[
\big||x|-|y|\big|=|x-y|;
\]
if \(xy<0\), then
\[
\big||x|-|y|\big|=|x+y|.
\]
Thus every solution must satisfy one of
\[
x=y+1,\quad x=y-1,\quad x=-y+1,\quad x=-y-1.
\]
Substitute each possibility into \(x+3y=3\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{Relation}&\text{Equation for }y&(x,y)\\ \hline
x=y+1&4y+1=3&\left(\frac32,\frac12\right)\\
x=y-1&4y-1=3&(0,1)\\
x=-y+1&2y+1=3&(0,1)\\
x=-y-1&2y-1=3&(-3,2)
\end{array}
\]
The pair \((0,1)\) appears twice and must be counted only once. For the three distinct candidates, the values of \((|x|,|y|)\) are
\[
\left(\frac32,\frac12\right),\quad (0,1),\quad (3,2),
\]
and each has absolute difference \(1\). They therefore satisfy both original equations.

Every possible solution was covered by the four cases, so there are exactly \(\boxed{3}\) ordered pairs, choice C.
